title: Freddie Jackson’s 15 Biggest Billboard Hits
summary: The hitmaker scored 10 R&B No. 1s and 19 top 10s in his career.
body: Despite overlapping career eras, Freddie Jackson wasn’t a blood relation to Michael or Janet, but he shared something with those superstars: a chart command of the 1980s R&B scene with a string of successful albums and singles that made him a dominant name in the genre’s landscape for nearly a decade. Born in Harlem, Jackson, whose death was announced Tuesday (Oct. 6) at age 70, began his musical journey in that hallowed training ground for many singers, church. At the White Rock Baptist Church of Harlem, Jackson fine-tuned his skills and forged a pivotal connection with Paul Lawrence, who later became a chief songwriting and producing collaborator. As he journeyed through the industry with various groups, he scored his biggest gig as a background singer for Melba Moore in the early 1980s. Jackson soon graduated to secure his own recording contract, and his 1985 debut, Rock Me Tonight , found instant acclaim. It debuted at No. 20 on the Top R&B/Hip-Hop Albums chart in May, and by the end of June, was No. 1 for the first of 14 eventual weeks in charge. Its songs scored similar success, as all four singles reached the top 10 on Hot R&B/Hip-Hop Songs : the title track and…

title: Will Taylor Swift Pass The Beatles for the Most Hot 100 No. 1 Hits?
summary: This week's Five Burning Questions looks at Swift inching ever-closer to the Beatles' benchmark of 20 Hot 100-toppers with this week's "Patient Zero."
body: With the release of the new quartet of Encore bonus tracks to her 2025 blockbuster The Life of a Showgirl , Taylor Swift picks up another four top five hits on the Billboard Hot 100 — including her 16th career No. 1 on the chart, with the single “Patient Zero.” “Zero” — which also received a star-studded music video debuted by Swift on MTV, while picking up the first-ever Artist Director award at September’s Video Music Awards — marks her third new No. 1 of the 2026 calendar year (after “Opalite” and “I Knew It, I Knew You”), as well as her fourth total to spend a week atop the chart (also including “The Fate of Ophelia,” in the last two of its 10 weeks at No. 1). Four is also the number by which Swift now trails The Beatles for the all-time record of Hot 100-toppers, with The Beatles’ benchmark of 20 No. 1s having stood unequaled for 56 years. How does “Patient Zero” fit with Swift’s 15 other No. 1s? And will she pass The Beatles’ historic mark soon enough? Billboard staffers answer these questions and more below. 1. title: Hope you like RCS, because Google Messages plans to remove this easy way to turn it off
summary: Google Messages could soon lose the ability to force SMS/MMS instead of RCS for each contact.
body: TL;DR Google Messages currently lets you disable RCS for conversations with individual contacts. A new app update appears to start laying the groundwork for this option’s removal. After that happens, your only option for avoiding RCS may be disabling it across all chats. Forgive us for sounding like a bit of a broken record at this point, but the arrival of Rich Communication Services (RCS) has been an absolute game-changer for Google Messages. It’s brought us everything from read receipts, to bigger media attachments, to cross-platform messaging with our iPhone buddies. That said, RCS isn’t without its own problems , but thankfully Messages has provided us with an easy way to opt out if it’s causing problems. Unfortunately, that now looks like it could be going away. You’re reading an Authority Insights story. title: Amazon stiffed you on a refund? You might be due a piece of this class-action settlement
summary: Most affected customers won't have to do anything to get a cut.
body: TL;DR Amazon has agreed to pay $309.5 million in a class action suit about incorrectly processed refunds. Affected customers should get restitution for incomplete refunds dating back to 2017. Amazon has also agreed to other measures, including temporary changes to its refund practices. Amazon is set to pay out more than $300 million to customers who claim the online gigaretailer’s return process failed them. Customers who received incomplete or late refunds, or no refunds at all, for returned items over the past nine years will be eligible to claim a piece of the settlement. As brought to our attention by Top Class Actions , Amazon has agreed to pay out $309.5 million to customers who weren’t correctly refunded for purchases made from September 5, 2017 to February 12 of this year. The suit claimed that Amazon’s return and refund practices violate Washington state law.

title: XGIMI’s wild new 4K projector finally has a US price
summary: Early buyers can knock hundreds off XGIMI’s new Google TV projectors.
body: TL;DR XGIMI has opened US reservations for the Aura 3 Max and Aura 3 Pro ahead of their October 20 Kickstarter launch. And while the retail numbers sit firmly in luxury-TV territory, early buyers can shave a chunky amount off the bill. The Max will start at $2,399 for Kickstarter backers, while the Pro will cost $2,199. Better yet, putting down a refundable $50 deposit through XGIMI knocks another $200 off, dropping the Super Early Bird prices to $2,199 and $1,999, respectively. XGIMI lists eventual MSRPs of $4,999 for the Max and $3,999 for the Pro.

title: Google could soon solve Pixel’s biggest face unlock flaw
summary: Android 17 QPR3 Beta 1 code points to a new "Face Active Illumination" feature in the works.
body: Credit: Joe Maring / Android Authority TL;DR Code within Android 17 QPR3 Beta 1 reveals Google is working on a “Face Active Illumination” feature, likely designed to assist face unlock in low light. Code clues suggest controls for a brightness scale, as well as toggles for bedtime, driving, dark environments, and Do Not Disturb. The feature likely uses display brightness rather than IR technology, though its connection to Google’s rumored Project Toscana couldn’t be ruled out. Google’s modern face unlock on recent Pixel flagships is Class 3 biometric certified, but as anyone who has tried unlocking their phone in a dim bedroom knows, it is practically useless once the lights go down. That shortcoming has long fueled anticipation around Google’s secretive Project Toscana , an effort to overhaul facial authentication across Pixel devices, Chromebooks, and presumably Googlebooks by extension. Now, new code discovered in Android 17 QPR3 Beta 1 reveals that Google is actively building a “Face Active Illumination” system to help solve face unlock’s low-light authentication woes. title: I loved using the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra, but I wouldn’t spend $2,000+ on it
summary: Is the Fold 8 Ultra the right foldable for you?
body: It’s not a hyperbole to say that the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra is one of the most powerful and capable folding phones available in the US this year. With its razor-thin design, outstanding displays, flagship Snapdragon chip, and oodles of One UI software features, it shouldn’t come as any surprise that the Fold 8 Ultra is about as robust as foldables come. However, the foldable world is more competitive than ever, thanks to both Samsung and its rivals, and that competition makes the Fold 8 Ultra difficult to be completely enamored with. The Fold 8 Ultra is a very good phone, and I certainly think there’s a decent audience for it, just as there always has been for Samsung foldables. But if it were my money going toward a folding phone in 2026, the Fold 8 Ultra wouldn’t be my first choice.

title: ESPN 4K HDR is showing up on Google TV, but users aren’t impressed
summary: The upgrade is spreading to more TVs, though the experience still looks rough.
body: TL;DR ESPN appears to have quietly expanded its 4K HDR support to Google TV, following its initial rollout on Apple TV last month. Early Google TV reports suggest the experience still needs work, with users complaining about choppy playback and HDR not triggering properly. ESPN launched its upgraded 4K HDR streams on iOS and Apple TV last month, promising more connected TV platforms would follow this fall. Now, Google TV users are seeing 4K HDR badges inside the ESPN app, suggesting the rollout has reached another major living-room platform. Unfortunately, getting the badge and getting the picture quality ESPN promised may be two very different things. In a recent Reddit thread , a TCL Google TV owner said an ESPN app update added 4K HDR labels to supported programming. But their TV never switched into HDR, while the picture looked choppy rather than sharper. Another Android TV user reported similarly poor playback, with frequent pauses during 4K events.

title: My favorite open-source Android screen mirroring app is now way faster
summary: scrcpy v5.0 brings GPU hardware decoding, native Windows on ARM support, and expanded audio capture.
body: TL;DR scrcpy v5.0 brings hardware decoding, which essentially shifts video decoding from the CPU to the GPU, reducing desktop CPU usage by up to 10x, saving power, and potentially lowering input latency. The v5.0 release also introduces official native Windows on ARM64 binaries optimized for Snapdragon-powered laptops. Other changes in this release include the ability to capture all audio streams in audio playback capture mode, improved video buffering, and fixes for UHID keypress dropping bugs. If you have ever needed to control your Android phone from your PC , chances are you rely on scrcpy (short for “screen copy”). The lightweight, open-source tool has long been the gold standard for screen mirroring your phone to your desktop over ADB, and its latest release makes it significantly more efficient. Developer Romain Vimont has officially released scrcpy 5.0 on GitHub , introducing native hardware-accelerated video decoding, official Windows on ARM64 binaries, and expanded audio capture options. The headline feature in scrcpy v5.0 is the switch to GPU-accelerated video decoding on the host machine. Up until now, scrcpy relied on software decoding via the computer’s CPU to proces…

summary: Everyone loves a budget smart home until excessive automation creates a mess.
body: Credit: Thanh Nguyen / Android Authority Building a cost-effective, entry-level smart home is an experiment that should come with careful planning and an emphasis on simplicity. Overengineering can cause frustration, particularly when your devices suddenly turn on or off out of nowhere, leaving you confused with a screen full of buttons and no idea where to tap. I only put my setup together with an IR blaster, two Android phones (you only need one if you don’t want a DIY home hub), a smart plug, and a couple of apps. Before configuring anything, I anticipated the project might become convoluted rather than convenient, so optimizing the control interface and day-to-day interactions was my priority throughout.

title: Your Meta glasses just got better at telling you where to go without pulling out your phone
summary: Turn-by-turn walking directions lead a bigger wave of Meta Glasses upgrades.
body: TL;DR Meta’s v128 update brings turn-by-turn walking navigation to Ray-Ban Meta glasses, along with Spatial Audio and other improvements. The newer v129 release follows with Mono Audio and Audio Balance accessibility controls. v129 is still rolling out gradually, while v128 appears to be much more broadly available. Pulling out your phone to check which way to turn somewhat defeats the point of wearing smart glasses . Meta tackled that problem last month with one of the more useful upgrades yet for its Ray-Ban smart glasses: turn-by-turn walking navigation. That feature arrived with the v128 update alongside several other improvements, and just as that release becomes more widely available, Meta is already following it up with v129 and a couple of new audio accessibility controls. The standout addition in v128 is pedestrian navigation, which lets you ask Meta AI for walking directions and hear turn-by-turn guidance through your glasses. For example, you can say, “Hey Meta, navigate to Times Square,” and the glasses will use location information from your connected phone to guide you there. For destinations too far to walk, Meta instead sends driving directions to your phone.

title: Google adds support for Markdown files in Google Docs and Drive
summary: Google is finally making life easier for people who prefer writing in Markdown.
body: TL;DR Google has finally added support for Markdown files in Google Docs and Drive. Users can now view, edit, and collaborate on Markdown files in Docs without converting them into a Doc format. Google Drive can also preview properly rendered Markdown files. Markdown is one of the best ways to write because it’s simple, straightforward, and relies entirely on the keyboard. This makes it easier to create well-formatted documents quickly without digging through thousands of menus. On the other hand, Google Docs is great for creating, editing, and viewing documents. Naturally, bringing the two together makes sense, and it seems Google has finally realized that. The company announced today that it’s introducing support for viewing, editing, and collaborating on Markdown files directly in Google Docs. If you’ve created a document in a Markdown editor like Obsidian, you can now import it into Docs and share it with your team. Docs will render the document with all Markdown formatting preserved, and collaborators can make edits without first converting the Markdown file into a Doc format.

title: Google’s latest Play Services update has a neat trick for your lost belongings

body: TL;DR Google’s October System Services update adds NFC support to Find Hub-compatible trackers, letting you tap a tag to quickly access its details or identify a lost tag. Setting up Find Hub trackers is getting easier, with options to name tags, choose categories, and enable features like Left-Behind Reminders during registration. The update also adds card artwork and payment network logos to card tokenization notifications, along with a smaller attribution change for apps using Google Maps features. Google just made Find Hub trackers a little harder to lose for good. The company has been steadily turning Find Hub into a much more capable alternative to other item-tracking networks. As part of Google’s October System Services updates , Google Play services v26.39 is adding NFC support for Find Hub-compatible tags. You’ll now be able to tap a tracker with your phone to quickly pull up its details and settings. More importantly, NFC can also help identify a lost tag, which could come in handy when something you’ve attached it to goes missing.

title: The first national ban on smart glasses could happen soon
summary: This country is considering a ban on smart glasses in some areas.
body: Credit: Meta TL;DR Norway’s government is proposing a temporary ban on smart glasses in some locations. The ban would apply to areas where “privacy is particularly important,” like schools, healthcare facilities, and fitness centers. The temporary ban would give the government time to decide which type of devices would be affected and whether permanent regulation is needed. Smart glasses are the hot new category that every major tech company is trying to jump on. Just last week, Samsung took one step closer to launching its first effort into the segment. However, as smart glasses continue to inch toward going mainstream, it’s becoming increasingly difficult to look past the growing concerns surrounding the technology, namely privacy. Now, one country is confronting those concerns by taking matters into its hands. According to The Associated Press , Norway is proposing a temporary ban on smart glasses. This would not be a blanket ban, but rather a ban in certain locations. It’s reported that the country wants the proposal sent to parliament “as soon as possible.”
